ai-&-i-by-every.name: AI & I by Every
ai-&-i-by-every.bio: Podcast: The SaaS Apocalypse Is a Goldmine With Figma’s Matt Colyer

html_en:
As AI capabilities surge forward, the industry is grappling with how to build for tomorrow while optimizing for today—from prompt engineering breakthroughs to infrastructure evolution to the ongoing "SaaS apocalypse" debate.

The Art of AI Prompting Gets Smarter

The conversation around prompt engineering is evolving beyond simple command-and-control. @swyx shared a deceptively simple but powerful insight about improving AI interactions:
"a smarter alternative to 'always use plan mode': always frame your task as a question, so that the model is invited to push back and rate the quality of the idea/suggest alternatives, rather than blindly execute what you SAID to do (which is often not precisely what you MEANT). literally just appending '?' to the end of your prompt often does it"
This represents a shift from treating AI as a passive executor to an active collaborator. Meanwhile, Peter Yang outlined a more systematic approach to building AI skills that improve over time, emphasizing context, evaluations, and memory systems that allow AI to learn from past interactions.

Infrastructure for the Agent Era

Behind the scenes, companies are rapidly building the plumbing for an AI-native world. Guillermo Rauch announced that agent filesystem state can now be "read, written and mounted independently of Sandbox lifecycle," describing it as "a novel virtual storage infrastructure solution" for all compute products. The focus on infrastructure extends to capabilities too. Rauch also highlighted the Skills API, positioning it as "the npm registry for agent capabilities and extensibility." This suggests we're moving toward standardized, composable AI capabilities rather than monolithic models. Anthropic made waves by doubling Claude Cowork usage limits for a month, with Boris Cherny noting that "Cowork is at its best on work that's too big for a chat: research across dozens of accounts, recurring reports, triaging my inbox and drafting replies."

Building for the Slope, Not the Point

Perhaps the most strategic insight came from @realmadhuguru, who warned against a common enterprise AI mistake:
"One of the most common mistakes I see enterprise AI teams make is building for today's model capabilities and price points. Think 6 months out. Models will be way smarter and cheaper. Scaffold around today's model weaknesses to push the frontier. Bet that the next generation of models will natively solve for the scaffold."
This "build for the slope" philosophy suggests that competitive advantage lies not in optimizing for current limitations, but in developing the capability to repeatedly identify and bridge model gaps as they evolve.

The SaaS Apocalypse Goldmine

The ongoing debate about whether AI will destroy traditional SaaS companies got a fresh perspective from Figma's Matt Colyer on Every's AI & I podcast. Rather than fearing disruption, Colyer sees massive opportunity:
"I think what's most exciting about this time is that I think it's gonna be like a billion [developers], maybe even more than that... I think there's this incredible time that we're moving through of product development and really the democratization of technology... there is dramatically more software out there in the world. If you're in that space, it means it's a gold mine."
Box CEO Aaron Levie provided a nuanced take on why coding agents haven't replaced human engineers despite having optimal conditions:
"Coding is basically the pinnacle of what you could reasonably automate with AI, and yet we still need human engineers to oversee agents for them to be effective... That's an incredible amount of benefits that AI coding agents get to work with... So if with all of that, engineers still remain in very high demand, the risks are going to be less than what's perceived for other areas of knowledge work."
The message is clear: AI augments rather than replaces, even in domains seemingly perfect for automation. As the infrastructure matures and capabilities expand, the companies positioning themselves to ride the wave of dramatically expanded software creation—rather than just defending against disruption—may find themselves in that goldmine Colyer described.
html_zh:
今天的AI行业充满了实用性的突破和深思熟虑的产品战略，从提示工程的小贴士到对SaaS工具未来的宏观思考，都体现了AI正在从实验性技术向日常工具的转变。

🎯 提示工程的新智慧

AI工程师们正在发现更聪明的交互方式。swyx分享了一个简单而深刻的见解：

"始终将任务框架为问题，这样模型被邀请推回并评估想法的质量/建议替代方案，而不是盲目执行你说的（这往往不是你真正想要的）。字面上只需在提示末尾添加'?'通常就能做到。"

这个看似微小的改变反映了AI交互设计的一个根本转变——从命令式转向协作式。与此同时，Peter Yang分享了构建自我改进AI技能的系统方法，包括添加上下文、触发器、评估和记忆系统。这些方法论表明，最有效的AI应用不是一次性的交互，而是经过深思熟虑设计的持续学习系统。

Claude Cowork的大胆押注

Anthropic将Claude Cowork的使用限制翻倍持续一个月，这是对其代理能力的重大押注。Boris Cherny解释说：

"Cowork在太大而无法通过聊天完成的工作上表现最佳：跨数十个账户的研究、定期报告、分拣我的收件箱并起草回复。"

💼 SaaS末日论的反击

一场关于AI对传统软件威胁的有趣辩论正在展开。Figma的产品管理总监Matt Colyer在Every播客中提供了令人信服的反驳：

"SaaS末日或软件的下一个时代，如果你愿意这样称呼的话。我对此非常兴奋，我认为Figma和许多其他SaaS业务也是如此。因为我认为全球开发者数量将达到十亿，甚至更多。如果你在这个领域，这意味着这是一个金矿。"

这种观点得到了Box CEO Aaron Levie的呼应，他指出即使在编程这个AI自动化的理想场景中，人类工程师仍然需要监督代理才能有效工作：

"编程基本上是你可以合理地用AI自动化的顶峰，然而我们仍然需要人类工程师监督代理才能使其有效。"

一位企业AI团队观察者提供了策略性建议：

"企业AI团队最常见的错误之一是为当今的模型能力和价格点构建。要考虑6个月后。模型将更智能、更便宜。围绕当今模型的弱点搭建框架来推动前沿。押注下一代模型将原生解决框架问题。"

🛠️ 开发者工具的新范式

Vercel的Guillermo Rauch展示了基础设施创新如何使AI代理更加实用，宣布了一个新的技能API：

"使用技能API让你的所有代理和平台更智能。把它想象成代理能力和扩展性的npm注册表。免费且开放。"

与此同时，@ryolu_演示了与Claude Composer的无缝设计工作流程，表明AI工具正在变得足够成熟，可以处理创意任务。

但也许最引人注目的是Garry Tan暗示的新项目：

"你现在终于可以尝试我几个月前开始工作的大项目之一了。我们希望这能随时间推移变得更擅长帮助你学习构建更好软件的最佳技术，更快。"

风投圈的自我反思

今天Twitter上出现了一个有趣的元对话，Matt Turck幽默地回应了关于风投的负面故事：

"现在X上正在传播关于风投的坏故事，但风投也有关于创始人的恐怖故事——比如，那次一个创始人决定接受另一个更高估值的条款清单，尽管我们明显有增值能力、思想领导力和供应商折扣。"

这种自嘲的幽默反映了科技界当前的紧张氛围，以及传统投资-创业关系在AI驱动的快速变化中面临的挑战。
